facts.name: Bee Balm
facts.light: Full sun, at least 6 hours; in shade it flowers less and gets more powdery mildew
facts.notes: Shaggy red, pink or purple flower heads that hummingbirds, bees and butterflies love. It spreads, so divide it every 2 to 3 years; plants given room and sun get less powdery mildew. Its lavender wild cousin is Wild Bergamot.

sources.title: English Gardens (Metro Detroit garden centers): Jacob Cline Beebalm
sources.note: Sold at English Gardens, one of many bee balm varieties there; red, about 4 ft tall, hardy to zone 3.

fall.why: if the leaves had powdery mildew (a white coating), bag them instead of composting. If they stayed clean, you can leave the stems for bees until spring

care.divideNote: Divide every 2 to 3 years so it doesn't get crowded; crowded plants get more mildew.

sources.title: Iowa State Extension: Growing Bee Balm in the Home Garden
sources.note: Bee balm does best in moist, well-drained soil in full sun (at least 6 hours); in part shade it flowers less and gets more powdery mildew. Flowers come in white, pink, red, lavender and purple.

sources.title: Iowa State Extension: Powdery mildew on bee balm
sources.note: Space bee balm 2 to 2½ ft apart in full sun, divide every 2 to 3 years, and remove infected plant debris in fall to cut down powdery mildew.

sources.title: Fine Gardening: Pink on pink (MSU Horticulture Gardens)
sources.note: Bee balm (Monarda didyma) grown at the Michigan State University horticulture gardens; hardy in zones 4 to 9.

sources.title: Penn State Extension: Cutting Down Perennials in the Fall
sources.note: Cut peonies, daylilies, brunnera and speedwell in fall; cut bee balm and garden phlox with powdery mildew and destroy the leaves; rake up hosta leaves (slug eggs); cut yarrow and Shasta daisy flower stalks but keep the base leaves. Leave grasses, Siberian iris, baptisia, sedum, Joe-Pye weed, coneflower, black-eyed Susan and most natives standing; leave marginally hardy anise hyssop tops over winter; tidy hardy geraniums, heucheras, hellebores and moss phlox in spring.

sources.title: Purdue Extension: Cut Back Perennials Now or Later?
sources.note: Cut iris in fall to reduce iris borer sites; cut peonies, bee balm and phlox; otherwise wait until several hard frosts have killed the tops.

companions.why: Combines well with purple coneflower, bee balm and native grasses; in gardens with Japanese anemones.
